question.text: A block of mass 2 kg sits on a rough horizontal floor whose friction coefficient is μ = 0.8. A horizontal force that grows with time, F = 2t newton (with t in seconds), pushes the block, as pictured. Using g = 10 m/s², sketch how the block's acceleration changes with time.
conditions: applied force is horizontal and time-varying, F = 2t newton

figure.description: A 2 kg block rests on a rough horizontal floor with friction coefficient μ = 0.8. A horizontal force F = 2t (F in newton, t in seconds) pushes the block to the right, increasing with time.

solution.approach: The block stays still until the growing force F = 2t exceeds the maximum friction, then it accelerates according to Newton's second law with that same friction opposing it.

steps.text: With only one μ given, the same value acts as both the static limit and the kinetic value once the block moves.
Find the time at which F first reaches this value; before that time the block does not move, so a = 0.
For t ≥ 8 s, the block slides, and kinetic friction (16 N, same value) opposes F; apply Newton's second law.
The full acceleration-time graph is flat at zero up to t = 8 s, then rises as a straight line of slope 1 starting from a = 0 at t = 8 s.
steps.equation: a = 0 for 0 ≤ t < 8 s; a = (t − 8) m/s² for t ≥ 8 s

final_answer.value: a = 0 for 0 ≤ t < 8 s; for t ≥ 8 s, a = (t − 8) m/s², a straight line starting at a = 0 when t = 8 s and rising with slope 1 m/s³ (no jump at t = 8 s, since the same μ gives the same friction immediately before and immediately after motion starts).

common_mistakes.text: Assuming motion starts at t = 0 and writing a = t − 8 for all t, giving a wrongly negative acceleration before t = 8 s.
Forgetting to subtract the friction force after motion starts and writing a = t (using F = 2t directly divided by mass without subtracting 16 N of friction).
